name: Hungarian
sources: Szende, Tamás (1994). Hungarian. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 24(2): 91-94.
Siptár, Péter; Törkenczy, Miklós (2000). The Phonology of Hungarian. Oxford University Press.
Gósy, Mária (2004). Fonetika, a beszéd tudománya. Budapest: Osiris.
Gósy, Mária (2001). The VOT of the Hungarian voiceless plosives in words and in spontaneous speech. International Journal of Speech Technology 4: 75-85.
Varga, László (2002). Intonation and Stress: Evidence from Hungarian. Palgrave Macmillan.
Kenesei, István; Vago, Robert M.; Fenyvesi, Anna (1998). Hungarian. Routledge.

Mády, Katalin; Reichel, Uwe D. (2007). Quantity distinction in the Hungarian vowel system: just theory or also reality? Proceedings of the 16th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences, Saarbrücken.
White, Laurence; Mády, Katalin (2008). The long and the short and the final: phonological vowel length and prosodic timing in Hungarian. Proceedings of Speech Prosody 2008, Campinas.

Markó, Alexandra; Juhász, Kornélia; Deme, Andrea; Gráczi, Tekla Etelka (2025). Formánselemzések a magyar magánhangzók jellemzésére a kezdetektől napjainkig: adatok és tanulságok. Nyelvelmélet és Nyelvleírás 1(1): 107-142.
Lehtonen, Jaakko (1970). Aspects of Quantity in Standard Finnish. Studia Philologica Jyväskyläensia VI. University of Jyväskylä. (quotes the older Hungarian vowel length ratio)
contrasts: vowel length in seven pairs; in a/á and e/é the members also differ in quality: short rounded [ɒ] against long [aː], short open-mid [ɛ] against long close-mid [eː]
consonant length (geminates) for nearly every consonant
voicing in stops, fricatives and affricates
palatal stops /c ɟ/ and palatal nasal /ɲ/ against dentals and velars
front rounded vowels /y yː ø øː/
allophony: regressive voicing assimilation in obstruent clusters, also across word boundaries (népdal with [bd], vízpart with [sp], azt with [st]); /v/ is devoiced by a following voiceless obstruent but does not voice a preceding one; /h/ devoices but is not itself voiced
/n/ takes the place of a following consonant: [m] before labials, [ɱ] before /f v/, [ɲ] before palatals, [ŋ] before velars
/h/ is [ɦ] between vowels, [ç] in a coda after a front vowel and [x] in a coda after a back vowel (ihlet, doh, pech); written final h is silent in some words (méh, cseh)
/j/ is a voiceless fricative [ç] after a voiceless obstruent at the end of a word (lépj, kapj) and a voiced fricative [ʝ] after a voiced one (dobj)
the palatal stops /c ɟ/ are often affricated

coalescence across morpheme boundaries: t or d plus j gives [cː] or [ɟː] (látja, adja), n plus j gives [ɲː], l plus j gives [jː]; t or d plus s gives [t͡ʃː] (barátság), t plus sz gives [t͡sː]; sz or z plus s gives [ʃː] (egészség, község)
geminates are shortened next to another consonant
long high vowels are often shortened when unstressed or word-final in colloquial speech
/p t̪ k/ are voiceless unaspirated; /b d̪ ɡ/ are fully voiced
/r/ is an apical trill, often a single tap between vowels
phonotactics: vowel harmony: suffix vowels agree with the stem in backness, and for some suffixes in rounding (-ban/-ben, -hoz/-hez/-höz); /i iː eː/ and often /ɛ/ are neutral
word-initial consonant clusters occur only in loanwords
short /o ø/ do not occur at the end of a word, where o and ö are always long
geminates occur between vowels and word-finally, not next to another consonant

stress.rule: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of every content word; articles, conjunctions and some particles are unstressed, and a preverb takes the stress of its verb; there is no regular secondary stress.
stress.cues: mainly pitch (the stressed syllable starts a falling movement) and intensity; duration plays little part because it carries the length contrast; no vowel reduction

rhythm.notes: Phrase-final lengthening of short vowels is limited, which keeps the length contrast in final position (White & Mády 2008).

length.notes: An older figure gives long vowels as twice the short ones (1 : 2, Laziczius 1966, quoted by Lehtonen 1970). Newer work finds smaller differences that depend on vowel height: in a carrier sentence short and long low vowels were separated by a gap between 100 and 130 ms and mid vowels met at about 100 ms, but short and long high vowels overlapped between 70 and 120 ms (Mády & Reichel 2007). Geminate voiceless stops in spontaneous speech are 1.4 to 1.5 times as long as single ones (total duration /p/ 101 and 137 ms, /t/ 95 and 143 ms, /k/ 98 and 143 ms); the difference lies in the closure, VOT stays the same (Neuberger 2015).

voice_onset_time_ms.notes: In carefully spoken isolated words the same study found 24.6, 26.6 and 50.2 ms. Neuberger (2015) found 22, 25 and 35 ms in spontaneous speech. /b d̪ ɡ/ are prevoiced.

intonation.declarative: each accented word starts a fall on its first syllable; successive falls start lower and lower, and the last one reaches the bottom of the range
intonation.yes_no_question: a question without the particle -e has a rise-fall on its last three syllables: low up to the antepenultimate syllable, peak on the penultimate, fall on the last; in shorter phrases the movement is compressed onto the syllables available
intonation.wh_question: falling from a high accent on the question word
intonation.continuation: rising or high level pitch at the end of a non-final phrase
intonation.accent_shape: H*+L: a fall that starts on the stressed first syllable

problems: there is no general voicing assimilation: it happens only where a rule in hu_rules names the word or cluster (azt, fogkefe), so népdal, vízpart, hatból, rakd, lakásban and megszeretteti keep the voicing of the spelling
/n/ is not assimilated before velars, palatals or b: ing, hangya and különben are spoken with [n]; only n before p becomes [m]
/h/ has one realisation: no [x] or [ç] in codas (doh, ihlet, technika), no [ɦ] between vowels, and the silent final h of méh is pronounced
/j/ after an obstruent at the end of a word stays a glide (lépj, kapj, dobj)
yes/no questions get the general rising question tune; the Hungarian rise-fall with its peak on the penultimate syllable is not modelled
some coalesced clusters lose their length (egészség is given a single [ʃ])
IPA output prints short a as [ɑ]; the sound used is a rounded back vowel, so this is a labelling fault
good: fixed initial stress without secondary stress
fourteen vowels with separate qualities for a/á and e/é
palatal /c ɟ ɲ/ and all four affricates
geminates, including doubled digraphs (ssz, ggy, tty, nny, ccs)
common coalescences are covered by rules (látja, adja, barátság, község)
unaspirated voiceless stops and a short trill for /r/
a very large rule and exception set for compounds and foreign names

notes: Vowel formant values are left out. Published Hungarian values differ widely with method, speaker and speech style (reviewed by Markó et al. 2025), and no single table could be checked for this profile.
